# The Things We Kept in the Depot

On the last Friday of every month, I baked whatever was in the freezer and called the bus drivers in to eat it. This was not an official duty. My official duty was lost property, but people left food on buses and the council had never issued a satisfactory instruction about it. I threw away anything with meat in it. Bread I could usually identify through the bag. The unmarked tubs I left alone until they became a problem for the next person.

For nineteen years there was no next person. Then the council sold the depot, and on a Thursday in April a man in a wool coat came to measure my shelves.

“Will these be coming with you?” he asked.

“Where am I going?”

He put his tape measure away. I think he’d been told that conversation had already happened.

The new depot would have a locker by the dispatch window. Anything too big for the locker would be photographed and disposed of after seven days. I was offered three mornings a week answering calls from home. The woman from Human Resources said I could do it in my pajamas. She meant this kindly, but I’d spent the first winter after my divorce going whole days in my pajamas and didn’t consider it much of a benefit.

I was given until the end of May to clear the room.

It was amazing what you could get rid of if you stopped believing its owner was on the way. The charity shop took thirty-one umbrellas, a mandolin, and a pair of roller skates with the original paper still stuffed inside. The man who bought scrap metal weighed the walking frames and offered me eleven pounds. I said I’d think about it. He said he’d be back on Tuesday, although neither of us believed he would.

The lemon tree came in on the number 8 on May 14. Ray carried it through dispatch with his jacket wrapped around the pot. There was soil all down his front.

“Someone’s going to want that back,” I said.

“You always say that.”

The tree was waist-high and had one lemon, green on the side that faced the window. Somebody had tied it to a bamboo stake with strips cut from an old shirt. There was a crack in the pot, neatly bridged with two loops of wire.

“An old bloke got on with it at the hospital,” Ray said. “I thought he’d get off at the garden flats, but he took it all the way to the exchange. I found it after I’d turned round.”

“Did you see him get off?”

“Saw him wait for me to lower the step. I assumed he had it.”

I wrote *tree, lemon, terracotta pot* in the book. The book was a duplicate pad left over from when a driver could hand a passenger a receipt for a parcel and carry it unaccompanied to the other end of the route. Sometimes a driver still did this, but only for somebody he knew.

By Wednesday the tree had dropped six leaves. I watered it. On Thursday it dropped nine, and I looked up what to do and discovered I shouldn’t have watered it. I moved it out of the draught. By Friday it had dropped so many that I stopped counting.

That afternoon my daughter, Alice, came to help me pack. She was thirty and had recently acquired a car big enough, she said, to make her popular with the wrong people. She brought two kinds of tape.

“Which boxes are going to yours?”

“None of them.”

She put down the tape. “I thought you wanted me to take your personal stuff.”

I showed her my personal stuff: a fork, a cardigan, one photograph of her on a donkey.

“God,” she said. “There was a woman behind that donkey charging by the minute. Do you remember?”

I remembered the woman chiefly because she had said there was no need to buy a photograph; we were welcome to take our own. I’d bought one anyway. Alice had been too old for the ride and wanted it so badly she’d tried to pretend she didn’t.

She slipped the picture out of its plastic stand and put it in her coat pocket. I almost asked for it back. Instead I asked how the new job was going.

“I didn’t take it,” she said.

I’d told three people she had.

“You sent me that message with the champagne glasses.”

“That was when they offered it.”

“Oh,” I said. “Well, you could have told me.”

“I just did.”

She opened a box and held the flaps together while I taped the bottom. We had always been good at the part that required two people and didn’t require talking.

The last person to claim anything in the ordinary way was a man who’d lost a shoe. He rang at nine in the morning and described it, including the square of cardboard he’d put under the insole. I found it in a bag marked *assorted trainers* and told him he could come before four.

“What about the other one?” he asked.

“You said you lost one.”

“I did. But I threw the other one out when I got home.”

He lived on the far side of town and understandably didn’t want to make the journey for a shoe he couldn’t use. We both stayed on the line a little longer than we needed to. Then he thanked me for finding it.

I put the shoe in the rubbish. At lunchtime I took it out again because the man had sounded as if he might change his mind. It sat on my desk for the rest of the week, taking up about as much room as my telephone.

The following Monday Ray brought in a note. Someone had handed it to him on the number 8. Written on the back of an appointment card were the words *Did the tree make it?*

There was a telephone number. I rang and got a man who said his name was Len.

“Yes, we’ve got it,” I said. “You can collect it any weekday before four.”

“I don’t want to collect it.”

“Well,” I said, “what do you want?”

There was a little scrape on the line, the sound of a telephone changing hands or a chair being dragged closer.

“I suppose I wanted to know where it ended up.”

I looked over at the tree. In the morning light the bare tips of the branches were almost white.

“Funny place to leave it,” I said.

“I tried the library first. They thought I was bringing it in for them to look after while I chose a book.”

“Were you?”

“No. But I did choose a book. Then I had to take that back as well.”

He’d moved out of his flat the previous week. His new room had a window that started six feet above the floor. He’d put a request on the noticeboard in the laundry asking whether anyone wanted the tree, but someone had taken it down to put up a warning about leaving things on the noticeboard.

I asked how old it was.

“Twenty-three. Older than any lemon tree you’d buy on purpose. Is the lemon still on it?”

“Yes.”

“Is it yellow?”

“Mostly.”

“You can have that,” he said.

After we hung up, I stood over the pot trying to get a finger under the wire without breaking it. There was a folded strip of rubber between the wire and the clay, protecting the rim. I’d never have thought to do that. I’d probably have used a new pot.

I rang Alice to see if she wanted a lemon tree. She said no, but asked why I was whispering.

“I don’t like talking on my mobile in the office.”

“Is there anybody else in the office?”

“No.”

She waited. I could hear something running in the background, perhaps a tap.

“Why didn’t you take the job?” I asked.

“Because it was in Bristol.”

“I thought you liked Bristol.”

“I do. I also like where I live now. I can like somewhere without moving there.”

She told me she’d worked out what the train would cost, and she’d actually gone as far as looking at rooms. One woman had wanted a deposit before Alice could see the place. Another had said she was welcome to use the kitchen as long as she didn’t cook anything that smelled like cooking.

“Why didn’t you ring me then?” I asked.

“Because you’d have found me a room.”

She wasn’t accusing me, which made it harder to say what came to mind. I got as far as “I could have,” and stopped.

“Yes,” she said. “I know.”

The tap, if it was a tap, went off. She asked what I was doing on Sunday. I said I wasn’t sure. She said she would come for lunch if I liked, but could we decide what to eat on the day? I said we could. When I hung up, it struck me that she might come and find there was nothing in the house. I made myself sit at the desk until the urge to write a shopping list passed.

On the last Friday, Ray brought sausage rolls from a bakery. He said he’d thought about putting them in an unmarked bag and leaving them on his bus for me to find, but he couldn’t trust the schoolchildren. We ate them with the door propped open. Without the shelves the room made a surprising amount of noise. We could hear a man in the yard reversing a bus and another man telling him, with steadily increasing disbelief, that he still had plenty of room.

At two o’clock, Len came in. I knew him because he looked straight at the tree. He wore a blue shirt with two mismatched buttons at the bottom, not that anyone would have noticed if he’d tucked it in.

“I said I wasn’t coming to collect it.”

“You did.”

He put a carrier bag on the desk. Inside were a handful of plant ties, a bottle with its label washed off, and a saucer big enough to take the pot.

“The chap downstairs always said he’d have that saucer when I was done with it,” he said. “Then when it came to it he only wanted it for his dog. The dog had a perfectly good bowl.”

I asked him to look at the leaves. He touched one of the remaining ones with the back of a finger.

“It doesn’t like moving,” he said. “It’ll do that again next time.”

“Will it live?”

“I don’t know. It always has.”

He bent to pick something out of the soil, a shred of foil that must have come from a cigarette packet. Then he straightened up and asked who was taking it.

I said I was.

Until I said it, I hadn’t known that I was. My flat had a shallow bay window, with enough room if I moved the small table on which I kept things I meant to take upstairs. Most of those things, on reflection, had been downstairs so long that upstairs could manage without them.

“Have you got help getting it there?” he asked.

I said I could call my daughter.

“Don’t lift it by the trunk,” he said.

We stood either side of the desk for a moment. He looked at the tree again, then picked up a sausage roll. He ate it neatly over the carrier bag, shook the crumbs into the rubbish, and left to catch his bus.

Alice came at four. She took one look at the pot and went out to get an old bath towel from the car. We wrapped it around the clay and carried the tree between us. Halfway across the yard she told me to stop. I said I was all right. She said she wasn’t asking whether I was all right; she had a bit of wire in her thumb.

We set the pot down. It was a tiny puncture, barely worth a plaster, but it bled quite freely. I handed her a clean tissue and waited while she pressed it to her thumb. Above us someone in dispatch had taped a piece of paper to the window saying *WE ARE STILL OPEN*. They’d have to go up there and peel it off in the morning.

“Did you get everything you wanted?” she asked.

I thought of the photograph in her coat pocket. I hadn’t seen it since she’d put it there and I didn’t know whether it was on her mantelpiece or still in the pocket, working its way through a hole in the lining.

“Yes,” I said.

We moved the tree the rest of the way with the wire on my side.

For the first two weeks at home, the lemon did nothing. Then one morning I found it on the carpet. It had landed on its stalk and made a little hole in itself. I rang Len to tell him. The number, it turned out, belonged to the desk at the place he’d moved to. A woman fetched him, and while I waited I heard her say, some distance from the telephone, “No, it’s the lady about your tree.”

I wondered how many calls he got that she could tell them apart.

“Was it yellow underneath?” he asked.

I turned it over. “Yes.”

“Well, there you are.”

I offered to bring him some. I meant a cake, or a jar of curd, something I could carry on the bus and present to him without either of us having to account for the journey. But he took me literally.

“How much lemon do you think there is?” he said.

After we’d hung up, I cut it across the middle. The skin was very thick and there wasn’t much inside. I squeezed half over some potatoes. The other half I left face down on a saucer until Alice came by.

She said she’d eat whatever I was having. It was too early for dinner and too late for lunch. We stood in the kitchen and ate the cold potatoes with our fingers. She squeezed the rest of the lemon over them, catching the pips in her palm, then rinsed her hands at the sink. I nearly told her that the lemon had taken almost a year to grow. Len hadn’t actually told me that. I’d read it somewhere and wanted it to be the sort of thing he’d know.

Outside, the number 8 went past. The route hadn’t changed with the depot, though the bus now made a left at the end of our street instead of a right. I still noticed every time. Alice didn’t look up. She was telling me about a woman at work who had gone on holiday and given her a key so she could water the plants. There were forty plants, she said. One of them had an instruction to be misted on alternate days, and the spray bottle was the size of a thimble.

“Have you done it?” I asked.

“Every other day since Tuesday.”

She went on to tell me which plant was her favorite. I thought it would be the one with the instructions, but it was an ordinary geranium on the landing. She hadn’t been asked to water that one. She didn’t even know if it belonged to the woman. It was just there each time she put the key in the door, and when she came out again she could tell by the smell that someone had beaten her to it.
